strengths: A well-formulated two-stage approach that bridges 4D scene geometry and video diffusion models to tackle key challenges in video object insertion (VOI), specifically user control, camera motion parallax, and dynamic occlusions.

The 4D-aware mask generation pipeline is technically sound: lifting the object into 3D, tracking local dynamics via lifted optical flow (SEA-RAFT), and reprojecting/segmenting via SAM 2 cleanly handles complex occlusions and dynamic object-scene interactions.

Clever formulation of the ROSE++ dataset by inverting the ROSE object-removal dataset (which removes both objects and secondary lighting/shadow effects) into an insertion dataset, paired with a multi-view VLM retrieval pipeline to obtain clean reference object images without copy-paste bias.

Extensive experimental validation, including quantitative metrics (VBench, CLIP-I, DINO-I), comprehensive component ablations (demonstrating the role of 4D masks, first-frame inpainting, and ROSE++ fine-tuning), and a detailed user study.
weaknesses: The baseline comparisons are exclusively against commercial black-box models (Pika-Pro and Kling). While comparing against commercial tools is valuable for industry-readiness claims, the paper omits comparisons against recent academic video insertion and propagation baselines discussed in related work (e.g., VideoAnyDoor, InVi, GenProp, or DreamInsert).

High pipeline complexity with compounded failure modes: the framework chains together multiple heavy foundation models (Uni4D, single-view 3D reconstruction, SEA-RAFT, SAM 2, OmniPaint, Wan2.1-VACE). The manuscript lacks a dedicated analysis of failure cases or cumulative error propagation when monocular depth/camera pose estimation or optical flow tracking fails in challenging scenes.

Minor editorial error: Section 4.3 in the main text refers to Table 3 when discussing the main quantitative benchmark results, which actually appear in Table 1 (Table 3 is the ablation study in the supplementary material).

strengths: Well-motivated integration of 4D geometric scene understanding with diffusion-based video generation, addressing long-standing failure modes in video object insertion such as geometry misalignment, scale drift, and occlusion handling.

Clever data curation strategy with ROSE++: repurposing an object removal dataset (ROSE) into an insertion dataset using VLM-based clean reference object retrieval elegantly provides supervised pairs with realistic shadows and ambient photometric interactions.

Decoupled pipeline design combining interactive 3D placement, scene-flow-guided 4D mask propagation, first-frame anchor generation, and video diffusion fine-tuning yields visually convincing, occlusion-robust results.

Comprehensive experimental validation, including VBench and identity metrics (CLIP-I, DINO-I), detailed ablations isolating each component's contribution, and a perceptual user study demonstrating significant advantages over prominent commercial tools.
weaknesses: Lack of comparisons against recent academic VOI baselines: Although relevant academic video object editing/insertion works (e.g., VideoAnyDoor, InVi, GenProp, DreamInsert) are discussed in the related work, the empirical evaluation solely compares against closed-source commercial text-to-video tools (Kling and Pika-Pro). Including at least one or two academic VOI baselines would provide a fairer and more rigorous assessment.

Computational complexity and pipeline runtime: The 4D reconstruction and propagation pipeline chains together several heavy foundation models (depth estimation, SEA-RAFT optical flow, single-view 3D point cloud reconstruction, SAM 2, Wan2.1-VACE-14B). The paper does not provide runtime/latency breakdowns, which is critical for evaluating commercial and interactive feasibility.

Limited discussion of failure modes and scene reconstruction fragility: Monocular 4D scene reconstruction and rigid object point cloud assumptions can fail under heavy non-rigid dynamic motion, extreme motion blur, or repetitive textures. A dedicated discussion of limitations and failure cases is needed.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in video editing: inserting objects into dynamic monocular videos while handling 3D/4D geometry, real-world occlusions, and realistic lighting/shadows.

The idea of inverting an object-removal dataset (ROSE) into an insertion dataset (ROSE++) by retrieving clean reference object images via VLMs and DINO ranking is creative and practical for training illumination-aware insertion.
The overall pipeline produces visually appealing results with coherent occlusion relationships and plausible shadow effects in several qualitative demonstrations.
Comprehensive qualitative and user study comparisons demonstrate clear improvements in geometric stability over purely prompt-guided commercial models.
weaknesses: Critical lack of academic baselines: The experimental evaluation only compares against commercial generative tools (Kling and Pika-Pro) conditioned on high-level text prompts. Comparing a dedicated, 4D-geometry-guided, mask-conditioned pipeline against black-box prompt-based text-to-video tools is inherently unfair. The paper fails to benchmark against state-of-the-art academic video object insertion methods cited in the related work, such as VideoAnyDoor, GenProp, InVi, or DreamInsert.

Limited algorithmic novelty and heavy reliance on pre-existing foundation models: The core framework is largely an engineering assembly of off-the-shelf components—Uni4D for scene reconstruction, pretrained single-image-to-3D for object points, SEA-RAFT for motion propagation, SAM 2 for mask tracking, an existing image inpainter for keyframe editing, and Wan2.1-VACE fine-tuned via LoRA. The technical innovation in the diffusion modeling itself is limited.

Evaluation scope and dataset size: VOIBench comprises only 50 video clips (100 total generated instances), which is relatively small for a benchmark intended to demonstrate production-level robustness across diverse real-world dynamics.

Writing and editorial errors: Several drafting issues detract from the paper's polish. For instance, in Section 4.3 the text refers to 'Table 3' when discussing the main quantitative baseline results (which are in Table 1), and Section 4.4 contains incomplete sentences (e.g., 'we observe that information such as the position of the person’s arm and scarf compared to the source video.').

Missing runtime and computational complexity analysis: The proposed multi-stage workflow combines multiple heavy foundation models (3D reconstruction, 4D scene estimation, optical flow, SAM 2, and a 14B parameter video diffusion model). The paper does not provide inference runtime, memory footprint, or pipeline latency analysis.

strengths: Addresses two critical and long-standing bottlenecks in video object insertion (VOI): 4D-aware geometric grounding under dynamic occlusions/moving supports, and synthesizing extended optical interactions (shadows, reflections) outside the explicit object mask.

The Optics-Aware Representation Alignment mechanism is technically neat and effective: by enforcing feature alignment with a stop-gradient extended-mask teacher branch during training, the network learns to render external optical phenomena at inference time using only the tightly-bound object mask.

The construction of the ROSE++ dataset is thoughtfully engineered, using multi-view rejection sampling via DINO embeddings to isolate clean reference images without leaking background or scene-dependent lighting shortcuts.

The 4D mask propagation module provides an intuitive and principled solution to handle moving surfaces (via KNN scene flow aggregation) and camera motion/occlusion handling (via 3D reconstruction, reprojection, and SAM 2).

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions on the newly curated VOIBench, featuring strong open-source and commercial baselines (Kling, Pika-Pro, VACE), clear ablation studies, attention map visualizations, and thorough user studies.
weaknesses: The overall pipeline is complex and heavily dependent on an extensive cascade of pretrained foundation models (Uni4D, TRELLIS, SEA-RAFT, SAM 2, OmniPaint, Wan2.1-VACE-14B). Failure or inaccuracies in earlier stages (such as monocular depth or pose estimation in challenging real-world footage) could cascade through to downstream synthesis.

Significant computational and runtime footprint: generating an 81-frame clip requires approximately 8.5 minutes on a state-of-the-art NVIDIA B200 GPU, which restricts practical usability for interactive workflows.

The reliance on synthetic/simulator-rendered datasets (ROSE++) for frame-differencing extended masks may have domain gap limitations when dealing with complex, real-world non-rigid illumination interactions (e.g., highly irregular caustic reflections or complex diffuse inter-reflections).
Requires manual 3D alignment and interaction in an initial anchor frame, representing higher user interaction overhead compared to simpler 2D bounding-box or point-prompt interfaces.

strengths: Addresses a crucial, long-standing dilemma in video object insertion (VOI): mask-free methods often modify unedited background regions and lack geometric control, whereas mask-conditioned models cannot synthesize physical optical interactions (e.g., cast shadows and reflections) that naturally extend beyond the object boundary.

The Optics-Aware Representation Alignment is an elegant and effective formulation: by distilling intermediate feature representations from an extended-mask teacher into the fine-mask branch via stop-gradient alignment, the model learns to anticipate and generate external optical effects during inference while strictly conditioning on a tightly bound object mask.

The 4D-aware mask generation pipeline thoughtfully couples 3D object lifting (TRELLIS), 4D scene reconstruction, and K-NN scene flow tracking to gracefully maintain object consistency over moving support surfaces and under complex foreground occlusions.

Solid dataset contributions: ROSE++ provides paired quadruplets specifically suited for supervised learning of optical effects without copy-paste shortcuts, and VOIBench offers structured evaluation axes across diverse scene types, occlusions, and lighting conditions.

Comprehensive experimental validation including standard quantitative metrics (VBench, CLIP-I, DINO-I), localized patch evaluations (Optics Mask vs. Object Mask PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), extensive ablations, and well-designed user studies.
weaknesses: Heavy multi-stage dependency: The 4D mask propagation relies on a complex cascade of separate models (UniDepthv2, SEA-RAFT, Uni4D, TRELLIS, and SAM 2), alongside an external image insertion model (OmniPaint) for first-frame anchoring. A failure or drift in any of these components (e.g., erroneous depth estimation or non-rigid scene flow tracking) could severely degrade downstream mask quality.

Substantial computational footprint: The inference time is approximately 8.5 minutes per 81-frame clip on an NVIDIA B200 GPU (4 min for 4D mask propagation + 4.5 min for the 14B diffusion backbone), with peak VRAM requirements of 48 GB, which may limit practical deployment and rapid interactive iteration.

Limited evaluation of the optics-aware alignment on non-synthetic/real-world ground truth: Quantitative validation of the optical side effects (Table 4, right) is performed exclusively on 25 held-out scenes from the synthetic ROSE++ dataset. It would strengthen the paper to evaluate or provide human/expert ratings specifically isolating shadow/reflection realism in complex real-world footage.

The quantitative impact of $L_{align}$ in the general VOIBench ablation (Table 3) is relatively marginal across global metrics (e.g., CLIP-I, DINO-I, Subject Consistency), indicating that standard video benchmark metrics struggle to capture fine-grained optical interactions.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: The paper effectively identifies and addresses two major bottlenecks in Video Object Insertion (VOI)—the lack of 4D geometric understanding for coherent temporal mask propagation and the inability of mask-conditioned diffusion models to render extended optical effects (such as cast shadows and specular reflections) beyond strict object boundaries.

Clever formulation for optics-aware synthesis: The proposed Optics-Aware Representation Alignment (using an extended mask branch with stop-gradient as a teacher during training) elegantly enables the diffusion model to synthesize realistic lighting and reflections beyond the foreground boundary during inference, without requiring the user to manually delineate shadow masks.

Principled 4D mask propagation: Decoupling static scene geometry from dynamic scene flow via KNN-based displacement aggregation provides robustness against moving support surfaces and occlusions, resolving common tracking drift issues found in purely 2D inpainting methods.

Comprehensive experimental validation: The authors conduct extensive comparisons against both state-of-the-art open-source methods and prominent commercial systems (Kling, Pika-Pro). The ablation studies (including attention map visualisations, feature alignment impacts, and paired shadow rendering metrics in Table 4) as well as the user studies provide solid support for the individual design choices.

Valuable dataset contribution: The creation of the ROSE++ quadruplet dataset, incorporating DINO-guided rejection sampling to isolate reference appearance from scene illumination, provides a useful resource for supervised training of optical interactions in video editing.
weaknesses: Cascading pipeline dependencies: The framework relies on a multi-stage orchestration of off-the-shelf foundation models (Uni4D, TRELLIS, SEA-RAFT, SAM 2, OmniPaint, Wan2.1-VACE). Failure modes in upstream components—such as monocular depth/camera pose inaccuracies, failure of image-to-3D lifting on complex shapes, or noisy optical flow on textureless surfaces—could cascade into mask deformation and degraded synthesis.

Heavy computational footprint and latency: As detailed in the supplementary material, running inference on an 81-frame video clip takes approximately 8.5 minutes (4 minutes for 4D mask generation and 4.5 minutes for synthesis) on an NVIDIA B200 GPU. This high computational requirement limits interactivity and real-time user feedback during editing.

Potential synthetic domain gap of ROSE++: Since ROSE is simulator-rendered, the optical interactions learned by the network may carry synthetic rendering biases; while real-world generalization is shown qualitatively, more analysis on diverse complex real-world illumination conditions (e.g., multiple conflicting colored light sources) would be beneficial.

User interaction complexity: Unlike prompt-driven or simple 2D bounding-box insertion tools, the pipeline requires users to manually manipulate 3D rotation, scale, and translation of a 3D proxy object in a 4D reconstruction viewer, adding substantial interaction overhead for non-expert users.
